butir.teks: The Book of Knowledge
It contains seven chapters. Chapter One: On the Virtue of Knowledge, Teaching, and Learning

Chapter Two: On the Individual Obligation (fard 'ayn) and the Communal Obligation (fard kifaya) among the Sciences, the Definition of Jurisprudence (fiqh) and Theology (kalam) as Part of the Knowledge of the Religion, and an Explanation of the Knowledge of the Hereafter and the Knowledge of This World
Chapter Three: On What the Common People Count among the Sciences of the Religion but Is Not Part of It, which includes an explanation of the kind of blameworthy knowledge and its extent
Chapter Four: On the Harms of Disputation, and the Reason People Busy Themselves with Disagreement and Argumentation
Chapter Five: On the Proper Conduct (adab) of the Teacher and the Learner
Chapter Six: On the Harms of Knowledge and of the Scholars, and the Distinguishing Marks between the Scholars of This World and the Scholars of the Hereafter
Chapter Seven: On the Intellect, Its Virtue, Its Divisions, and the Reports That Have Come Concerning It
Chapter One: On the Virtue of Knowledge, Teaching, and Learning, and Its Evidence from Transmitted Sources and from Reason
Chapter Two: On Praiseworthy and Blameworthy Knowledge, Their Divisions and Their Rulings

It contains an explanation of what is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) and what is a communal obligation (fard kifaya), an explanation of how far the place of theology (kalam) and jurisprudence (fiqh) extends within the knowledge of the religion, and the preference of the knowledge of the Hereafter.

An explanation of the knowledge that is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn). The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim," and he (peace and blessings be upon him) also said, "Seek knowledge even if it is in China." People differed about the knowledge that is obligatory upon every Muslim, and split over it into more than twenty groups. We will not lengthen the text by reporting the details, but the sum of it is that each group applied the obligation to the knowledge it is itself occupied with. The theologians (mutakallimun) said it is theology (kalam), since by it the affirmation of Divine oneness (tawhid) is grasped and the Essence of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and His attributes are known. The jurists said it is jurisprudence (fiqh), since by it acts of worship, the lawful and the forbidden, and which transactions are forbidden and which are lawful are known; and by this they meant what individuals need, excluding rare occurrences. The exegetes and the hadith scholars said it is the knowledge of the Book and the Sunna, since through the two all the sciences are reached.
The Sufis said that what is meant by it is this knowledge. Some of them said it is the servant's knowledge of his state (hal) and his station (maqam) with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Some of them said it is knowledge of sincerity, of the diseases of the selves, and of distinguishing the prompting of the angel from the prompting of Satan.
Some of them said it is the knowledge of the inner, and that is obligatory upon particular groups, who are the people of it; and they turned the wording away from its generality.

Abu Talib al-Makki said it is the knowledge of what is contained in the hadith that includes the foundations of Islam, which is his saying (peace and blessings be upon him), "Islam is built upon five: the testimony that there is no god but Allah (١)" up to the end of the hadith, because what is obligatory is these five, so it is obligatory to know how to act in them and how the obligation applies.

What the one who verifies should be certain of and have no doubt about is what we will now mention: knowledge, as we set forth in the preface of the book, is divided into the knowledge of conduct ('ilm al-mu'amala) and the knowledge of unveiling ('ilm al-mukashafa), and what is meant by this knowledge is only the knowledge of conduct. The conduct that the sane, adult servant is charged with performing is three things: belief, action, and abstention. So when a sane man reaches puberty, by emission or by age, at mid-morning of a day for example, the first thing obligatory upon him is to learn the two phrases of the testimony and understand their meaning, which is the saying "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." It is not obligatory for him to attain the unveiling of that for himself through reasoning, investigation, and the refinement of proofs; rather it suffices him to affirm it as true and believe it firmly, without any flicker of doubt or agitation of the soul. That can come about through mere imitation (taqlid) and hearing, without investigation or demonstration, since the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) was content, from the rough Bedouin Arabs, with affirmation and declaration, without their learning a proof (٢)

When he has done that, he has fulfilled the obligation of the time, and the knowledge that is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) upon him at that time is learning the two phrases and understanding them. Nothing beyond this is required of him at that time, as evidenced by the fact that if he died right after that he would die obedient to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, not disobedient to Him. Anything else becomes obligatory only through incidental circumstances that arise, and that is not necessary in the case of every person; rather it is conceivable that a person be free of them. Those circumstances are either in action, in abstention, or in belief.

As for action: he may live from mid-morning of his day until the time of the noon prayer, so that with the entry of that time it newly becomes incumbent on him to learn purification and the prayer. If he is healthy and is such that, were he to wait until the time when the sun passes its zenith, he would be unable to complete the learning and the performance within the time, but the time would run out if he busied himself with learning, then it is not far-fetched to say that the apparent presumption is that he will remain alive, so it is obligatory for him to bring the learning forward before the time.

It may also be said that the obligation of the knowledge that is a condition of the act comes after the obligation of the act, so it is not obligatory before the sun passes its zenith. And likewise for the remaining prayers. If he lives to Ramadan, the obligation of learning about fasting newly arises because of it: that its time is from dawn to sunset, that what is obligatory in it is the intention and abstaining from eating, drinking, and intercourse, and that this continues until the sighting of the new moon or two witnesses. If he acquires wealth anew, or had wealth at the time of his puberty, it is obligatory for him to learn what zakat is incumbent on him; but it is not required of him immediately, rather it is required of him only at

the completion of the year from the time of his Islam. If he owns only camels, he is required only to learn the zakat of camels, and likewise for the other categories. When he enters the months of the pilgrimage (hajj), he is not required to hasten to the knowledge of the pilgrimage, since performing it may be delayed, so learning it is not immediate. But the scholars of Islam should alert him that the pilgrimage is an obligation that may be delayed, upon everyone who owns provisions and a mount, if he is indeed an owner, so that perhaps he sees prudence for himself in hastening. At that point, if he resolves upon it, it is required of him to learn how the pilgrimage is performed, and he is required to learn only its pillars and obligations, not its supererogatory acts. If his doing of that is supererogatory, then his knowledge of it is also supererogatory, so learning it is not an individual obligation (fard 'ayn). Whether it is forbidden to remain silent about alerting him to the obligation of the pilgrimage itself at once is a matter for consideration befitting jurisprudence (fiqh). And such is the gradual progression in the knowledge of all the other acts that are an individual obligation.

As for abstentions, it is obligatory to learn the knowledge of them according to what newly arises in his situation, and that differs with the condition of the person, since the mute is not obliged to learn what speech is forbidden, nor the blind what looking is forbidden, nor the Bedouin the dwellings in which sitting is forbidden. So that too is obligatory according to what the situation requires: what is known to be something he is free of, learning it is not obligatory; and what he is engaged in, he must be alerted to it, as if at the time of his Islam he was wearing silk, or sitting on usurped property, or looking at someone who is not a mahram, then it is obligatory to inform him of that. And what he is not engaged in but is about to encounter soon, such as eating and drinking, then it is obligatory to teach him, so that if he is in a land where wine is drunk and pork is eaten, it is obligatory to teach him that and alert him to it. And whatever it is obligatory to teach him, it is obligatory upon him to learn.

As for beliefs and the works of the hearts, knowledge of them is obligatory according to passing thoughts (khawatir): if a doubt occurs to him about the meanings that the two phrases of the testimony indicate, it is obligatory for him to learn what leads to the removal of the doubt.
